Here's what he actually said — and why it changes everything.", "author": "699e12d16ef041f10a195450", "item-category": "69c08fd080415a7553051e0c", "tabs": [ "69c22206c7ede1d4fc6a5fa1", "69c09dca3cac7986ad2990b4", "69c0900d385ce2c1be1ae158", "69c085d28383a3710d83adf6", "69c33aae5e60542e77d08f86", "69c085ddd46b33b7eed0d1f7", "69c0a0d2dad175912e825b7b" ], "main-content": "

I have a neighbor I don't know. He passes my building most mornings on Howard Street — same time, same direction, same preoccupied pace. I've never learned his name. I've never made a real effort to.

I tell myself this is fine. San Francisco is a city of polite strangers. People here mind their own business, and that is considered a form of respect.

But then I read what Jesus said, and I can't quite settle back into comfortable.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus looks at his listeners and says something that should have cleared the room: love your enemies. Not tolerate them. Not forgive them when you feel ready. Love them — actively, concretely, in a way that costs you something.

\"You have heard that it was said, love your neighbor and hate your enemy. But I tell you: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.\"

He's not describing an emotion. He's describing a practice. And then, in the same breath, he raises the bar even further: if you love only the people who love you back, what exactly are you doing that anyone else isn't?

That's the question I keep tripping over.

Because the natural thing — the obvious thing — is to love people who love you back. Loyalty, affection, belonging: all of it runs on reciprocity. You return my calls and I return yours. You show up for me and I show up for you. This is not a character flaw. It's how most human relationship works.

What Jesus describes is something else. It's love directed toward people who haven't earned it, who won't return it, who may actively oppose you. Not as a one-time act of heroism — as a way of living.

If you love only the people who love you back, what exactly are you doing that anyone else isn't?

I don't think I do this well. Most days I love the people who are easy to love. I stay kind with people who stay kind with me. And the stranger on Howard Street? I walk past him at the same time every morning and we have never once exchanged names.

Perhaps that's where this starts — not with enemies, but with the ordinary people I've decided not to see. The ones who don't make demands, so I never have to consider them. The ones who are present but invisible in my daily life.

Jesus seems to suggest that the reach of our love says something real about us. Not who we are at our best, on our best days, toward our best people. But who we are toward everyone else.

That's still unresolved for me. But I think it's worth walking with — the next time I'm on Howard Street.
